pos: n. (Caspar Hedio, 1494–1552, cathedral preacher of Strasbourg and church historian)
etymology: German Caspar, from Persian, treasurer; Hedio, a grecised form of the surname Heid, heath.
biblical_def: Caspar Hedio preached in Strasbourg cathedral for nearly thirty years and was the steadiest of the three men who carried that city's Reformation. Capito had the learning and Bucer the diplomacy; Hedio had the pulpit and the patience. He came in 1523, preached through the transition from the mass to the evangelical service, held the cathedral congregation together through the Anabaptist pressure of the 1520s and the imperial pressure of the 1540s, and gave his spare years to history. He translated Eusebius and the other early historians into German and continued the chronicle to his own time, on the conviction that a church which does not know what it came from will be told what it came from by its enemies. That is the whole argument of Protestant historical writing in its first generation: the Reformation was not an innovation but a return, and the record would show it to anyone who could read it. Hedio put the record in the language of the people who needed it. Paul states the duty plainly: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time, and preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects.
webster_full: CHRON'ICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects.
CATHE'DRAL, n. The see or seat of a bishop; the principal church in a diocese.
TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; interpretation.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Joe 1:3
Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Strasbourg's cathedral preacher, who put the church's own history into German.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the charge Hedio spent his life answering and which is still made: that the Reformation invented a new religion in the sixteenth century. He answered it the only way the charge can be answered, by putting Eusebius and the rest into German where a literate burgher could check for himself what the church of the first four centuries had taught and what it had not.

The principle to recover is that the handing down of what God has done is a command laid on each generation, and that it is a command about telling, not merely about believing. “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). Joel makes the chain explicit and gives it four links: “Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation” (Joe 1:3). A church history written in the vulgar tongue is that verse carried out with a press.

pos: n. (Katharina Schütz Zell, 1497–1562, wife of the Strasbourg reformer Matthew Zell)
etymology: Greek Katharina, from katharos, pure; German Schütz, an archer; Zell, a cell, a hermitage.
biblical_def: Katharina Schütz Zell was a Strasbourg citizen's daughter who married Matthew Zell in 1523, when a priest's marriage was still a public scandal, and who spent the next forty years at the work a minister's wife does when the city is full of fugitives. She ran what amounted to an open house: Strasbourg took in waves of refugees from the peasant risings, from the French persecutions, from the imperial reconquest of the south German cities, and a great many of them ate at her table. She nursed through plague. She wrote — a defence of clerical marriage when her husband was attacked for it, letters of comfort to the widows of men killed in the Kentzingen rising, and a small hymnbook drawn from the Bohemian Brethren, published in cheap parts so that a labouring family could buy one at a time. Her writing is pastoral and domestic in the exact sense: it is addressed to households. She never held office, never claimed one, and never preached; what she did was open a door, set a table, and put a psalm into the hands of people who had lost everything. “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the practice of receiving and entertaining strangers without reward, and succour as aid afforded in distress.
webster_full: HOSPITAL'ITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, with kindness and liberality.
SUC'COUR, n. Aid; help; assistance; particularly, assistance that relieves and delivers from difficulty or distress.
REF'UGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety.
MA'TRON, n. An elderly married woman, or an elderly lady.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
Tit 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
corruption_summary: A pastor's wife in a refugee city: an open table, a nursed plague, and a cheap hymnbook.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is a modern reading that cannot see the work for what it is. Because Katharina wrote and argued in print, she is enlisted as a frustrated clergywoman born too early, and her actual labour — hospitality on a scale that kept families alive, nursing, consolation of widows, hymns for poor households — is treated as the lesser thing she settled for. That inverts her own account. She defended her husband's office and never sought it, and the writings that survive are a wife's, a neighbour's, and a nurse's.

The principle to recover is that Scripture assigns this labour real weight and names women by name for it. Paul commends Phebe as “a succourer of many, and of myself also” (Rom 16:2), and the older women in Crete are charged to be “teachers of good things” (Tit 2:3) to the younger women in the household, which is a commission, not a consolation prize. The open door is apostolic: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2). A city full of refugees is where that verse costs something.

pos: n. (Johannes Sturm, 1507–1589, rector of the Strasbourg gymnasium and schoolmaster of Protestant Europe)
etymology: German Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Sturm, a storm, a tempest.
biblical_def: Johannes Sturm built the school that every Protestant school copied. Called to Strasbourg in 1537, he gathered the city's scattered Latin schools into one graded gymnasium of nine classes, each with a stated end and a stated book, running from the elements of grammar to rhetoric and the reading of Scripture in the original tongues. His stated aim was a wise and eloquent piety: godliness first, then the learning to think, then the power to say it plainly. The school drew pupils from across the continent and the plan went everywhere — into the Jesuit colleges that opposed it, into the German gymnasia, into the English grammar schools, and by way of its graduates into Geneva and Scotland. Sturm had his failures. He held on too long, quarrelled bitterly with the Lutheran clergy of the city over the Supper, and was finally forced out at eighty-four after half a century. The institution outlasted the quarrel. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gymnasium as a place of exercise, also a school, and eloquence as the art of speaking with fluency and propriety.
webster_full: GYMNA'SIUM, n. A place where athletic exercises are performed; a school; a place where the youth are instructed.
EL'OQUENCE, n. The art of speaking well, or of expressing thought with fluency, force and propriety.
CUR'RICULUM, n. A course; particularly, a stated course of study in a seminary of learning.
PI'ETY, n. Piety in principle, is a compound of veneration or reverence of the Supreme Being and love of his character.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
corruption_summary: The Strasbourg gymnasium and its programme: a wise and eloquent piety.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the three things Sturm insisted on holding together. Piety without learning turns into sentiment; learning without piety turns into vanity; and both without eloquence stay locked in the head of the man who has them. Sturm's order mattered as much as his list: godliness first, because a school that reverses the order produces clever men who cannot be trusted with what they know.

The principle to recover is that plain speech is a duty and not a gift some teachers happen to have. Paul puts it in the bluntest terms available: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). Speaking into the air is what unschooled eloquence does, and a nine-class grammar course is simply the long way of obeying that verse. The promise behind the labour is Solomon's: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6).

pos: n. (Jakob Sturm von Sturmeck, 1489–1553, statesman of Strasbourg)
etymology: German Jakob, from Hebrew Yaaqob, a supplanter, one who takes by the heel; Sturm, a storm.
biblical_def: Jakob Sturm was not a minister and is the reason Strasbourg had a Reformation at all. A patrician of the city, trained in the humanities, he entered the magistracy in 1524 and for nearly thirty years was the man Strasbourg sent whenever something had to be settled — to the diets, to the league negotiations, to the colloquies. He represented the city at Speyer where the protest was lodged, carried the Tetrapolitan Confession to Augsburg in 1530 when the four south German cities could not subscribe the Saxon article on the Supper, held Strasbourg inside the Schmalkaldic League, and after the league was crushed negotiated the terms that kept the city from being sacked. He also backed Johannes Sturm's school with the city's money and his own weight, which is why it existed. He is the type of the Christian magistrate as the Reformation understood the office: not a theologian, not a churchman, but a man in authority who uses the authority to make room for the preaching of the word and then stands out of the pulpit. “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines magistrate as a public civil officer invested with the executive government, and statesman as a man versed in the arts of government.
webster_full: MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
STA'TESMAN, n. A man versed in the arts of government; usually, one eminent for political abilities.
PA'TRICIAN, n. A nobleman; in Roman affairs, a person of rank, descended from the ancient senators.
DI'ET, n. An assembly of the states or circles of the empire of Germany.
scriptures: Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
corruption_summary: The magistrate who made room for the preaching and never climbed into the pulpit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in two directions and Sturm's career answers both. On one side, the magistrate who treats the church as a department of the city and appoints its doctrine; on the other, the churchman who treats the magistrate as an embarrassment and will take nothing from him. Strasbourg had its share of the first error — the council sometimes overreached — but Sturm himself held the line a Christian statesman is supposed to hold.

The principle to recover is that civil authority is a real ministry with a stated and limited commission. “For he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) grants the office, and the closing words of that clause bound it. What the church asks of the magistrate is stated modestly: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). A city gets that or it does not, and Solomon names the difference: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2).

pos: n. (Ambrosius Blarer, 1492–1564, reformer of Constance and of Württemberg)
etymology: Greek ambrosios, immortal, divine; German Blarer, a Constance patrician surname.
biblical_def: Ambrosius Blarer entered the Benedictine house at Alpirsbach as a boy, rose to be its prior, read Luther, and walked out in 1522 to preach in his native Constance. He is the reformer of the whole upper Swabian country: Constance first, then Memmingen, Esslingen, Lindau, Isny, Ulm, and finally Württemberg, where Duke Ulrich sent him with Erhard Schnepf to reform the duchy — Blarer in the south with the Swiss view of the Supper, Schnepf in the north with the Lutheran, a division of ground that worked better than anyone expected. When Charles V took Constance in 1548 and returned it to Austria and the mass, Blarer lost his city and spent his last sixteen years as a pastor in Swiss villages. He wrote hymns throughout. He is a useful figure because his life refuses the tidy map: a monk who became a reformer, a south German who held a Swiss doctrine, a man who reformed a duchy and died in a village. Paul's charge to the Corinthians states the whole of it: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prior as the superior of a convent of monks, and exile as banishment, the state of being expelled from one's country.
webster_full: PRI'OR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
REF'ORMER, n. One who effects a reformation or amendment; one of those who commenced the reformation of religion.
DU'CHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
corruption_summary: The prior who walked out of the cloister and reformed upper Swabia, and lost his city at the end.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of measuring a ministry by whether its institutions survived. By that measure Blarer failed: Constance was taken, the mass restored, and the reformer finished his life in borrowed parishes. The congregations he had taught did not stop believing when the emperor's troops arrived, and the Württemberg church he helped order outlived him by centuries.

The principle to recover is that the promise attached to the work is about the work, not about the tenure. “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is given to men who will not see the result, and the clause before it is a double command to stand still under the load. Hebrews describes the outward look of such lives without apology: “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38), and prefaces it with the verdict that the world was not worthy of them.

etymology: Greek Thomas, from Aramaic teoma, a twin; German Blarer, a Constance patrician surname.
biblical_def: Thomas Blarer was the younger brother of Ambrosius and did in the council chamber what his brother did in the pulpit. He studied at Wittenberg, boarded in Melanchthon's house, and came home to Constance to enter the city's government, rising to burgomaster. The two brothers carried the city together through the whole evangelical period: the abolition of the mass, the ordering of the schools and the poor relief, the long refusal to subscribe the Lutheran article on the Supper, the alliance with the Swiss cities, and the final catastrophe when Charles V put Constance under the imperial ban in 1548 and the city was handed back to Austria. Thomas lost his office and his city and lived out his life on his estate. What the brothers built in Constance is the pattern the south German cities followed: a magistracy and a ministry that each kept to its own work and met on the matters that belonged to both — schools, the relief of the poor, the suppression of open scandal. “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines burgomaster as the chief magistrate of a municipal town, and council as an assembly of men summoned to advise.
webster_full: BUR'GOMASTER, n. A burgh-master; the chief magistrate of a municipal town in Holland, Flanders and Germany.
COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
CIT'IZEN, n. The native of a city, or an inhabitant who enjoys the freedom and privileges of the city.
BAN, n. In the German empire, a public censure by which the privileges of a member are suspended.
scriptures: Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
corruption_summary: The burgomaster brother: the council chamber half of the Constance Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a city's reformation is the work of its preachers and that the magistrates are either patrons or obstacles. Constance shows the truer arrangement. One brother preached and one brother governed, and neither did the other's work; the schools, the poor chest and the public order were settled by men who had to balance a civic budget, and the doctrine was settled by men who had to answer for it in a pulpit.

The principle to recover is Nehemiah's, which is the plainest account of a city rebuilt by divided labour under one mind: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6). The civic calling is not a lesser version of the ministerial one. Jeremiah lays it on exiles who had no political power at all: “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7).

pos: n. (Johannes Zwick, c. 1496–1542, pastor and hymnwriter of Constance)
etymology: German Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Zwick, from Middle High German, a peg, a nail.
biblical_def: Johannes Zwick was a doctor of laws who gave up the law for the ministry and became, with the Blarer brothers, the third of the men who reformed Constance. He wrote the city's church order and much of its poor relief, and he put together the Constance hymnbook, one of the first south German collections meant for a whole congregation rather than a choir. Several of its hymns are his own, and they are written the way a pastor writes when he knows who will be singing: short lines, plain words, the doctrine carried in the verse rather than hung on it. He died in 1542 at Bischofszell, where he had gone to minister in a plague, and caught what he was tending. That is the fact his hymns are now read through, and rightly. A man who writes about the brevity of life and then goes into an infected town has signed his own verse. The apostle gives the office both halves: a song to sing, and a flock to feed whatever it costs. “Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jam 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plague as a malignant contagious fever, and hymn as a song of praise to God.
webster_full: PLAGUE, n. Any malignant disease, particularly the oriental or Levantine plague, a contagious and very malignant fever.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God.
CONTA'GIOUS, a. Catching; that may be communicated by contact, or by a subtle effluvia.
PAS'TOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
scriptures: Jam 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: Constance's hymnbook, and the pastor who died of the plague he went into.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse concerns congregational song rather than the man. A hymnbook is now largely a matter of taste, selected for the feeling it produces in the people who choose it. Zwick compiled one as an act of pastoral teaching: the book was the congregation's doctrine in a form they could carry home and sing without a cleric present, which is why the verse is plain and the lines are short.

The principle to recover is that singing is instruction, and the apostle says so without hedging: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). Teaching and admonishing — the two verbs are the pulpit's. James assigns the song its occasion alongside prayer: “Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jam 5:13). A pastor who sets his people singing has preached to them twice.

pos: n. (Memmingen, an imperial free city of upper Swabia and an early evangelical city)
etymology: Old High German Mammingin, the settlement of Mammo's people; a place-name of the Swabian plain.
biblical_def: Memmingen was a small imperial free city on the Swabian plain whose Reformation ran ahead of almost everyone's. Christoph Schappeler was preaching evangelical doctrine from St Martin's by 1513; the council abolished the mass in 1528; the city subscribed the Tetrapolitan Confession at Augsburg in 1530 with Strasbourg, Constance and Lindau, and joined the Schmalkaldic League. It is remembered for something else as well. In the spring of 1525 the assembled peasants of upper Swabia met in Memmingen and issued the Twelve Articles, the most famous document of the German peasant risings, which demanded the right of each congregation to choose its own preacher, relief from the small tithe and from new labour services, and an end to serfdom — each claim set out with scripture references in the margin. Some of the grievances were just and the city's own preachers had taught the men to read the Bible that they now cited. The rising itself was rebellion, it was crushed, and the Reformation in the south bore the blame for a generation. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).

corruption_summary: The Swabian free city of the Tetrapolitan Confession, and of the Twelve Articles of 1525.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption attached to Memmingen is the reading of the Twelve Articles as a Christian charter of revolution, which they are regularly made to be. The articles cite Scripture in the margins and some of their complaints were honest: a congregation does have an interest in who preaches to it, and new burdens had been laid on men who could not bear them. But a just grievance does not create a right of armed revolt, and the margin references do not make the rising biblical. The articles asked for what they wanted and the peasant armies went and took it.

The principle to recover is that Scripture addresses both the grievance and the remedy, and it does not confuse them. Oppression is condemned throughout the prophets, and the magistrate who rules wickedly is told his end. But the subject's duty is stated without a loophole for a worthy cause: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). What the church is told to seek from the state is modest and lawful: “a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2).

etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; German Schappeler, from a dialect word for a maker of garlands.
biblical_def: Christoph Schappeler was a St Gallen man who became preacher at St Martin's in Memmingen in 1513 and was preaching evangelical doctrine there before Luther's theses were posted. He attacked the tithe, the purchase of masses and the exactions laid on the poor, and he did it from the pulpit of a city whose weavers and labourers were in exactly the condition he was describing. In 1525 he was closely involved in the drafting of the Twelve Articles of the upper Swabian peasants, and when the risings were crushed he had to flee to St Gallen, where he lived another twenty-six years as a respected minister. His case is the hardest in the south German Reformation and it should be stated plainly rather than tidied. He preached what Scripture says about the oppression of the poor, which is a great deal, and he lent his pen to a document that the peasant armies carried into a rebellion. The first was his duty. The second was a failure of the distinction between declaring God's judgment on an injustice and authorising men to avenge it themselves. The sword belongs elsewhere: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God” (Rom 13:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sedition as a commotion or insurrection against public tranquillity, and oppression as the act of overburdening by cruelty or injustice.
webster_full: SEDI'TION, n. A factious commotion of the people, a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration of justice.
OPPRES'SION, n. The act of oppressing; cruelty; a burdening with unreasonable impositions.
GRIEV'ANCE, n. That which causes grief or uneasiness; a wrong done and suffered.
EXAC'TION, n. The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay; an unjust demand.
scriptures: Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Jam 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
corruption_summary: The Memmingen preacher who named the oppression truly and lent his pen to a rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption runs both ways on Schappeler and both ways are worth naming. Modern writing on the peasant war enlists him as proof that the gospel is a programme of social revolt, which requires ignoring Rom 13 and the whole apostolic settlement of the subject's duty. The opposite error, commoner in conservative accounts, is to treat the grievances as inventions and the preaching against tithes and exactions as agitation, which requires ignoring the prophets.

The principle to recover is that Scripture gives the church a loud voice against oppression and no sword to back it with. The magistrate holds the sword as God's minister: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). The preacher holds a word, and may spend it freely on a wicked ruler — “when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2) is Scripture, not sedition. What he may not do is hand the sword to the congregation.

pos: n. (Wendelin Rihel, d. 1555, printer of Strasbourg)
etymology: German Wendelin, a diminutive of Wendel, a wanderer; Rihel, an Alsatian surname.
biblical_def: Wendelin Rihel ran one of the great evangelical presses of the Upper Rhine. From the 1530s his Strasbourg shop printed Bucer's commentaries and church-order writings, the works of the city's ministers, schoolbooks for Johannes Sturm's gymnasium, and in 1539 the second and much enlarged Latin edition of Calvin's Institutes — the edition in which that book first took something like its mature shape, printed while its author was an exile preaching to the French congregation in the same city. Rihel also printed the French Institutes of 1541 and a stream of Bibles and devotional works. A printer of this kind is not a tradesman who happens to handle theology; he chooses what will exist. Every book in his list was a decision about what the churches of a whole region would be able to read, made at his own risk and his own cost, in a trade where a seized edition could ruin a house. “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth” (Ecc 12:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines press as a machine for printing, and edition as the publication of a book, the whole number of copies published at once.
webster_full: PRESS, n. A machine for printing; called a printing-press.
EDI'TION, n. The publication of any book; also, the whole number of copies of a work published at once.
IM'PRINT, v. To mark by pressure; to print; to stamp names, words or figures on paper.
TY'POGRAPHY, n. The art of printing; the operation of impressing letters and words on forms.
scriptures: The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Col 4:16
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.
Rev 1:3
Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand.
corruption_summary: The Strasbourg press that printed Bucer and the 1539 Institutes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern assumption that the means of publication are neutral plumbing. They never have been. Rihel chose a list, and the churches of the Upper Rhine read what he chose; a printer in Paris in the same decade was choosing differently and men were burned over the difference. Whoever controls what can be multiplied controls what a region can be taught.

The principle to recover is that God has always attached a blessing to the circulation of the written word and has commanded it as a labour, not left it to the market. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2) is about legibility and distribution together. Paul tells one congregation to pass its letter to the next and to read the one coming back (Col 4:16), which is a publishing instruction. And the blessing is pronounced on the reader and the hearer alike: “Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy” (Rev 1:3).
